aeo.what_is: Persistent eating of non-food substances like dirt, paper, or ice, causing medical risk or impairment.

description.overview: Pica is characterized by persistent eating of non-nutritive, nonfood substances for at least one month, at an age where this behavior is developmentally inappropriate, not culturally sanctioned, and sufficiently severe to warrant clinical attention. Substances vary by individual and context (e.g., dirt, clay, paper, hair, chalk, ice, paint, metal, detergent).
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A child with autism repeatedly eats paper, chalk, and dirt from the playground despite redirection, requiring constant supervision to prevent ingestion.
A pregnant woman craves and eats ice constantly throughout the day, going through multiple trays daily, and is later found to have severe anemia.
A toddler eats paint chips from an old house, leading to elevated blood lead levels and developmental concerns.
A teen with intellectual disability chews and swallows clothing fabric and plastic items, resulting in emergency room visits for intestinal blockages.
An adult under chronic stress begins eating large amounts of cornstarch daily, hiding the behavior and experiencing GI distress.
A young child eats handfuls of dirt from the garden regularly, and lab work reveals iron deficiency and intestinal parasites.
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Confusion about why the cravings feel so strong and hard to resist.
Relief when iron or zinc deficiency is identified and treated, reducing cravings.
Shame or embarrassment about the behavior, especially in older children and adults.
Concern about medical complications like poisoning, obstruction, or infection.
Frustration with needing constant supervision to prevent ingestion.
Hope that behavioral interventions can help reduce or eliminate the behavior.

content.description: Pica is characterized by persistent eating of non-nutritive, nonfood substances for at least one month, at an age where this behavior is developmentally inappropriate, not culturally sanctioned, and sufficiently severe to warrant clinical attention. Substances vary by individual and context (e.g., dirt, clay, paper, hair, chalk, ice, paint, metal, detergent).
content.temporal_criteria: Persistent eating of nonfood substances must occur for at least 1 month. Transient or exploratory mouthing in toddlers does not meet criteria. The behavior must be inappropriate for developmental stage and not part of culturally sanctioned practices. Severity is based on frequency, medical risk of ingested substances, and level of supervision required.
content.misdiagnosis_explained: Pica is often missed because it's attributed to normal developmental exploration in toddlers without considering age-appropriateness and persistence. Ice eating (pagophagia) is commonly dismissed as a habit rather than screened for iron deficiency. In individuals with intellectual disabilities or autism, pica may be normalized as part of the condition rather than assessed as a distinct, treatable problem. Pica can be overdiagnosed when culturally sanctioned practices (geophagia in some communities) are pathologized, or when transient stress-related behaviors are labeled without persistence. The key distinction is persistent, developmentally inappropriate ingestion that causes medical risk or functional impairment.
content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Persistent eating of non-nutritive, nonfood substances for ≥1 month. B. Eating is inappropriate to developmental level. C. Not part of culturally supported or socially normative practice. D. If occurring in the context of another mental disorder (e.g., ASD) or medical condition (e.g., pregnancy), it is sufficiently severe to warrant independent clinical attention.
content.prevalence: More common in children, individuals with intellectual disability or autism, and during pregnancy; true prevalence varies by setting and definition.
content.age_of_onset: Often begins in childhood; can occur in adolescence or adulthood (including pregnancy).
content.prognosis: Course depends on underlying causes and access to treatment. Correcting nutritional deficiencies and implementing behavioral/environmental interventions often reduce behavior; risk persists without supervision in neurodevelopmental conditions.

mechanisms_hypotheses: Micronutrient deficiencies (iron, zinc) may alter appetite/interoception and drive pagophagia or geophagia.
Reward/sensory-seeking processes (insula and striatal circuits) maintain habit loops via texture/taste reinforcement.
In neurodevelopmental conditions, reduced inhibitory control and sensory modulation differences can increase risk.
neurobiology.risk_context: Higher rates with iron-deficiency anemia, pregnancy, chronic stress/trauma, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, and in environments with lead paint or contaminated soil.

history_environment: Detailed description of ingested items, frequency, settings, triggers, supervision level, and access to hazardous materials.
Exposure history (lead paint, soil, pica among peers), cultural practices, and safety incidents (choking, obstruction, poisoning).
medical_assessment: Vitals and physical exam (dental erosion/damage, abdominal tenderness, bowel changes).
Labs: CBC with indices, ferritin, iron studies; zinc level when available; basic metabolic panel; blood lead level when risk/exposure suspected; pregnancy test when relevant.
Stool O&P if contaminant/parasite exposure; celiac screen if malabsorption suspected.
Imaging (abdominal X-ray/CT) for suspected obstruction/bezoar or foreign body ingestion.
standardized_measures: Functional behavior assessment (FBA) and ABC logs to identify maintaining variables (automatic/sensory, attention, escape, tangible).
Screen comorbid symptoms: PHQ-9/GAD-7, autism/ID profiles, OCD scales when indicated.
differential_diagnosis: Normal mouthing in toddlers (developmentally typical, transient).
Culturally sanctioned ingestion (e.g., geophagia) without impairment/toxicity.
Obsessive–Compulsive Disorder (ingestion to reduce obsessional anxiety).
ARFID with sensory-based exploration (without persistent nonfood ingestion).
evaluation.team_and_process: Coordinate among primary care/pediatrics, psychiatry/psychology, dietetics, and when needed GI/toxicology; include school/caregivers for environmental controls.

behavioral: Repeated ingestion of nonfood items despite redirection.
Preference for specific textures (chalky, crunchy, earthy) or temperatures (e.g., ice).
physical_complications: GI obstruction or bezoars, constipation, dental damage.
Lead or other heavy-metal toxicity, parasites, infections.
Nutritional deficiencies, weight loss or failure to thrive in children.
triggers_maintainers: Attention from caregivers or escape from tasks.
Boredom, anxiety, or lack of structured activity.

severity_levels.mild: Infrequent ingestion with low-to-moderate risk items; responds to supervision and basic strategies.
severity_levels.moderate: Weekly ingestion or access to hazardous items; medical monitoring needed; structured behavioral plan required.
severity_levels.severe: Frequent ingestion, high-toxicity or obstructive items; recurrent medical complications; requires intensive supervision and multidisciplinary management.

psychological: Anxiety, trauma exposure, sensory modulation differences

impact_on_life.home: Need for locked storage and environmental proofing; caregiver stress.
impact_on_life.school_work: Supervision demands, restricted activities/placements for safety.
impact_on_life.medical: ER visits for obstruction/toxicity; dental and GI complications.
impact_on_life.social: Stigma and reduced participation in community settings.

medical_nutritional: Correct identified deficiencies: oral/IV iron for iron-deficiency anemia; zinc supplementation when deficient; treat parasites and GI complications.
Dietitian-guided plan to optimize macro/micronutrients and regular meals/snacks.
behavioral_environmental: FBA-informed plan targeting function of pica.
Differential reinforcement (DRA/DRI) to reinforce safe oral alternatives (e.g., chewable jewelry, crunchy foods) or incompatible behaviors.
Response blocking/interruption and prompt fading in high-risk contexts.
Noncontingent access to sensory substitutes (safe chew items) and high-engagement activities.
Stimulus control: lock hazardous items, clean environments (vacuuming, covers for outlets/peeling paint), supervision schedules.
Caregiver/teacher training for consistent implementation and data tracking.
psychotherapy: CBT components for older children/adults to address urges, anxiety, and coping; habit reversal elements where feasible.
Psychoeducation about risks and safety routines.
medications: Treat co-occurring conditions that may maintain behavior (e.g., SSRIs for OCD/anxiety; melatonin for sleep which can reduce nighttime access).
Consider N-acetylcysteine (off-label) for repetitive behaviors in neurodevelopmental contexts (evidence mixed; specialist-guided).
school_and_care_plans: Safety IEP/504 accommodations (increased supervision, safe seating, access to alternative chew items, task engagement).
Environmental audits and staff training; crisis protocols for suspected ingestion.

treatment_goals: Eliminate ingestion of nonfood substances and prevent medical complications.
Correct nutritional deficiencies and improve overall health.
Increase engagement in safe, functional activities and oral alternatives.
Build caregiver/school capacity for consistent prevention and rapid response.
Generalize gains across home, school, and community settings.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Assuming behavior is developmentally typical mouthing in children without considering age and persistence.
Attributing pagophagia to preference rather than screening for iron deficiency.
Overlooking pica in individuals with ASD/ID due to communication barriers or constant supervision masking ingestion.
overdiagnosis_factors: Culturally sanctioned ingestion mislabeled as disorder despite minimal impairment/toxicity.
Transient stress-related or exploratory behaviors without persistence or harm.
Confusing nail-biting or non-ingestive oral habits with pica.

specifiers.note: Specify medical sequelae (e.g., lead toxicity, obstruction) and supervision level required.

warning_signs: Abdominal pain/distention, vomiting, constipation or bloody stool (possible obstruction).
Neurologic symptoms, anemia, or developmental regression (consider lead toxicity).
Dental fractures/erosion; sudden interest in paint, soil, or sharp objects.
self_help_strategies: Remove/lock hazardous items; use childproof locks and high storage.
Provide safe oral alternatives (sugar-free gum, chewable jewelry) and high-engagement activities.
Structured routines with supervision during high-risk times; keep hands busy (fidgets).
Address constipation and ensure regular meals/snacks to reduce sensory/physiologic drivers.

early_childhood: Beyond typical mouthing age, persistent ingestion of nonfood items; respond with environmental control and reinforcement of safe behaviors.
school_age: Geophagia or ingestion of classroom materials; school plan with supervision, safe seating, and DRA to alternative items.
adolescence_adulthood: Stress- or deficiency-related cravings; CBT components, deficiency correction, and harm-reduction strategies.
pregnancy: New-onset pagophagia or geophagia; screen/treat iron deficiency; obstetric and nutritional co-management.

first_person_statements: I craved ice constantly during pregnancy. I'd go through trays and trays every day. It turned out I was severely anemic.
I know eating dirt isn't normal, but the urge is so strong I can't resist. I feel embarrassed and worried about getting sick.
My son with autism kept eating paper and plastic. It was terrifying—we had to watch him every second to keep him safe.
After I started iron supplements, the ice cravings just disappeared. I couldn't believe it was that simple.
I'd eat cornstarch by the spoonful when I was stressed. I hid it from everyone because I knew it was weird.
Learning that pica could be treated with behavioral therapy and addressing my iron deficiency gave me so much hope.

real_life_examples: A 6-year-old boy with autism and intellectual disability repeatedly eats paper, chalk, and small plastic items at school. A functional behavioral assessment (FBA) reveals that the behavior is maintained by automatic/sensory reinforcement—the texture and taste are rewarding. The school team implements a plan with differential reinforcement of alternative behaviors (DRA), offering crunchy snack alternatives (pretzels, carrot sticks) on a schedule, and response blocking when he reaches for nonfood items. Environmental modifications include removing access to paper/chalk and providing safe chewable jewelry. After 8 weeks, pica incidents decrease to near zero, and he engages more with appropriate snacks and activities.

A 28-year-old pregnant woman develops intense cravings for ice, consuming multiple trays daily and chewing ice constantly. She feels tired and short of breath. Her obstetrician orders labs and finds severe iron-deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, ferritin 5 ng/mL). She begins oral iron supplementation (ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily) and increases dietary iron. Within 3 weeks, the ice cravings (pagophagia) resolve completely, her energy improves, and follow-up labs show rising hemoglobin. Her doctor explains that pagophagia is a common manifestation of iron deficiency and monitors her closely throughout pregnancy.

A 14-year-old girl with anxiety begins eating small stones and pebbles from her backyard when feeling stressed about school. Her parents notice the behavior after she complains of abdominal pain, and an X-ray shows multiple foreign bodies in her GI tract. She's referred to a psychologist who diagnoses pica in the context of anxiety. Treatment includes CBT to address anxiety triggers, coping skills like deep breathing and journaling, and stimulus control (supervised time outdoors, garden off-limits). Her pediatrician monitors labs (normal) and GI symptoms. After 3 months, the behavior stops, and she uses healthier coping strategies for stress.

A 4-year-old living in an older home with peeling paint is found to have elevated blood lead levels (15 mcg/dL) during a routine screening. Her parents report she's been eating paint chips. The health department inspects the home and finds lead-based paint. The family temporarily relocates, the home is remediated, and the child receives chelation therapy under toxicology guidance. A behavioral plan includes constant supervision, removing access to peeling areas, and redirecting to safe activities. Her lead levels decrease, and developmental monitoring continues. The family receives education about lead poisoning prevention.

A 19-year-old with longstanding pica (geophagia—eating clay and dirt) since childhood seeks help after experiencing chronic abdominal pain and constipation. Labs show iron deficiency and a stool test reveals intestinal parasites. She's treated with iron supplementation, antiparasitic medication, and a behavioral therapist helps her identify triggers (boredom, sensory seeking). She begins using safe oral alternatives (crunchy vegetables, sugar-free gum) and engages in structured activities. After 4 months, her cravings decrease significantly, her GI symptoms resolve, and she maintains regular follow-up with her doctor.

comparisons.similarities: Both involve putting non-food items in the mouth.
comparisons.differences: Normal mouthing is a transient, age-appropriate exploratory behavior in infants and toddlers (typically under 2 years) and resolves naturally. Pica involves persistent ingestion (not just mouthing) of non-nutritive substances beyond the age where it's developmentally expected, lasting at least 1 month and causing medical or functional concerns.

comparisons.similarities: Both can involve repetitive, ritualistic behaviors that are difficult to resist.
comparisons.differences: In OCD, ingestion of non-food items may occur to reduce obsessional anxiety (e.g., contamination fears, magical thinking). In pica, ingestion is driven by cravings, sensory seeking, or automatic reinforcement, not obsessions. Treatment approaches differ—OCD focuses on exposure and response prevention for obsessions, while pica targets nutritional deficiencies and behavioral reinforcement.

comparisons.similarities: Both are feeding and eating disorders that can involve limited intake or unusual eating patterns.
comparisons.differences: ARFID involves avoidance or restriction of food intake (not eating enough or variety of food) due to sensory issues, fear, or lack of interest—without ingesting non-food substances. Pica involves eating non-nutritive, nonfood items. The two can co-occur but are distinct conditions.

comparisons.similarities: Both may involve eating non-food items.
comparisons.differences: In psychotic disorders, ingestion may be driven by delusions (e.g., believing an item has special powers) or command hallucinations. Pica is not associated with psychosis and is instead driven by cravings, sensory preferences, or nutritional deficiencies. Assessment of thought content and perception helps differentiate.

faqs.question: Is pica just a bad habit?
faqs.answer: No. Pica is a recognized feeding and eating disorder that can have serious medical consequences. It's often driven by underlying factors like iron or zinc deficiency, sensory-seeking behaviors, neurodevelopmental conditions, or stress—not simply a bad habit. It requires evaluation and treatment.

faqs.question: Why do people eat ice constantly?
faqs.answer: Persistent ice eating (pagophagia) is commonly associated with iron-deficiency anemia. The exact mechanism isn't fully understood, but treating the iron deficiency typically resolves the ice cravings. If you or someone you know eats ice compulsively, get labs checked for anemia.

faqs.question: Can pica cause serious health problems?
faqs.answer: Yes. Depending on what's ingested, pica can cause lead poisoning, intestinal blockages or bezoars, parasitic infections, dental damage, poisoning from toxic substances, and nutritional deficiencies. It requires medical evaluation and monitoring.

faqs.question: Is pica more common in children with autism or intellectual disabilities?
faqs.answer: Yes. Pica is significantly more common in individuals with autism, intellectual disabilities, and other neurodevelopmental conditions due to sensory-seeking behaviors, reduced inhibitory control, and communication challenges. It requires tailored behavioral interventions and close supervision.

faqs.question: How is pica treated?
faqs.answer: Treatment includes correcting nutritional deficiencies (iron, zinc), behavioral interventions (functional behavior assessment, differential reinforcement, response blocking), environmental modifications (locking hazardous items, supervision), and treating co-occurring conditions (anxiety, OCD). A multidisciplinary team is often needed.

faqs.question: Will my child outgrow pica?
faqs.answer: Some young children do stop as they develop, especially if it's mild and related to a treatable deficiency. However, persistent pica, especially in the context of neurodevelopmental disorders, often requires intervention and may not resolve without treatment. Early intervention improves outcomes.

faqs.question: What should I do if I catch my child eating something dangerous?
faqs.answer: Stay calm, gently remove the item if safe to do so, and assess what was ingested. Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) or seek emergency care if the substance is toxic, sharp, or causing distress. Document the incident and follow up with your pediatrician for evaluation and a safety plan.

faqs.question: Can pregnant women have pica?
faqs.answer: Yes. Pica during pregnancy is relatively common and often involves ice (pagophagia), clay (geophagia), or starch (amylophagia). It's frequently associated with iron deficiency. Pregnant women with pica should be screened for anemia and receive nutritional counseling and prenatal care.

faqs.question: Is eating ice harmful?
faqs.answer: Eating ice occasionally isn't harmful, but compulsive ice chewing (pagophagia) can damage teeth and is often a sign of iron-deficiency anemia. If you're craving and eating ice constantly, see a healthcare provider to check your iron levels.

faqs.question: What is geophagia?
faqs.answer: Geophagia is the practice of eating earth, soil, or clay. It's sometimes culturally sanctioned in certain communities and may be related to mineral deficiencies. When it causes medical problems (parasites, lead exposure, GI obstruction) or functional impairment, it meets criteria for pica and should be evaluated.

faqs.question: Can stress cause pica?
faqs.answer: Stress can be a trigger or maintaining factor for pica, especially in individuals with underlying vulnerabilities (neurodevelopmental conditions, anxiety, sensory-seeking tendencies). However, stress alone doesn't cause pica—it usually involves a combination of biological, psychological, and environmental factors.

faqs.question: How do I keep my child safe if they have pica?
faqs.answer: Environmental control is key: lock or remove hazardous items (cleaning supplies, paint, small objects), supervise closely, create a safe play area, provide safe oral alternatives (chewable jewelry, crunchy snacks), and work with a behavioral specialist on a reinforcement plan. Regular medical monitoring is also important.

faqs.question: Can pica be a sign of something more serious?
faqs.answer: Yes. Pica can signal iron or zinc deficiency, lead poisoning, intestinal parasites, or co-occurring conditions like autism, intellectual disability, OCD, or psychosis. It warrants a thorough medical and behavioral evaluation to identify and treat underlying causes.

faqs.question: Is pica the same as eating disorders like anorexia or bulimia?
faqs.answer: No. Pica involves eating non-food substances and is not driven by body image concerns or fear of weight gain. Anorexia and bulimia involve restriction, binge eating, and/or purging motivated by weight and shape concerns. Pica is a separate feeding and eating disorder with different causes and treatment.

faqs.question: Can behavioral therapy really stop pica?
faqs.answer: Yes. Behavioral interventions based on functional behavior assessment (FBA)—like differential reinforcement of alternative behaviors, response blocking, and stimulus control—are very effective, especially when combined with correction of nutritional deficiencies and environmental modifications. Success depends on consistency and caregiver/school involvement.

faqs.question: What labs should be checked for someone with pica?
faqs.answer: Common labs include: complete blood count (CBC) with iron studies (ferritin, serum iron), zinc level, basic metabolic panel, blood lead level (if exposure suspected), and stool tests for parasites if geophagia or contaminated substance ingestion is present. Your doctor will tailor testing based on what's being ingested.

faqs.question: Can pica occur in adults without intellectual disabilities?
faqs.answer: Yes. Adults with normal cognitive function can develop pica, often related to iron deficiency (pagophagia), pregnancy, chronic stress, or psychiatric conditions (OCD, psychosis). It's less common but still requires evaluation and treatment.

faqs.question: What is a bezoar and how does it relate to pica?
faqs.answer: A bezoar is a mass of undigested material that accumulates in the GI tract, potentially causing obstruction. People with pica who ingest hair (trichophagia), fibers, or other indigestible substances are at risk for bezoars, which may require endoscopic or surgical removal.

faqs.question: Can medications help with pica?
faqs.answer: No medication treats pica directly. However, medications can address co-occurring conditions (SSRIs for OCD/anxiety, iron supplements for anemia) or support behavioral treatment. The most effective approach is correcting deficiencies, behavioral interventions, and environmental controls.

faqs.question: How long does it take for pica to improve with treatment?
faqs.answer: It varies. Pagophagia related to iron deficiency often resolves within weeks of starting supplementation. Behavioral interventions for sensory-driven or automatic pica may show improvement within weeks to months with consistent implementation. Longstanding or severe cases may take longer and require ongoing support.

content.when_to_seek_help: Immediate medical care for signs of obstruction, poisoning (e.g., lead exposure), choking, severe abdominal pain, or vomiting. Clinical evaluation is warranted for persistent nonfood ingestion, especially with anemia, dental damage, weight loss, or infection risk.

positive_factors: Identification and correction of iron/zinc deficiency
Consistent FBA-informed behavioral plan with caregiver/school training
Safe environment with limited access to targets and enriched activities
challenging_factors: Severe neurodevelopmental impairment with high sensory drive
Environmental lead/contaminant exposure or low supervision
Longstanding behavior with conditioned reinforcement and medical sequelae

tiles.title: What is Pica?
tiles.summary: Persistent eating of non-food substances like dirt, ice, paper, or paint causing medical risk.

tiles.title: Signs & Symptoms
tiles.summary: Eating non-nutritive items, cravings for specific textures, GI obstruction, poisoning, and dental damage.

tiles.title: Causes & Risk Factors
tiles.summary: Iron or zinc deficiency, pregnancy, neurodevelopmental disorders, sensory seeking, and environmental exposure.

tiles.title: How It's Diagnosed
tiles.summary: History of ingestion, lab work for deficiencies and toxicity, functional assessment, and medical exam.

tiles.title: Treatment Options
tiles.summary: Correct nutritional deficiencies, behavioral interventions, environmental controls, and medical monitoring.

tiles.title: Medical Complications
tiles.summary: Lead poisoning, intestinal obstruction, parasites, dental damage, and anemia.

tiles.title: Recovery & Prognosis
tiles.summary: Good outcomes with deficiency correction and behavioral therapy. Supervision and consistency are key.

tiles.title: Living with Pica
tiles.summary: Environmental safety, supervision, safe oral alternatives, and addressing nutritional and behavioral triggers.

tiles.title: Getting Help
tiles.summary: Seek evaluation for persistent non-food ingestion, signs of poisoning, obstruction, or anemia.
